text: With FSBB, the admission criteria for post-secondary pathways will no longer be determined by streams but by subject levels and performance of students.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Changes to the polytechnic admissions criteria will recognise a wider profile of learners and provide them with more options.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: We are also reviewing the Polytechnic Year 1 criteria to better recognise the different subject levels taken by our students.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: In order to prepare our learners, ITE will expand their Work-Study Diplomas (WSDips) and Technical Diplomas (TDs) offerings to allow students to deepen their skills and competences through a more hands-on pedagogy.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: I encourage ITE students to make full use of the opportunities, given the positive employment outcomes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: We will continue to encourage more of them to make use of these opportunities.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: For primary and secondary schools, MOE recognises the importance of equipping students with a strong foundation in Mother Tongue Languages.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: This will enable our students to appreciate our heritage and culture, and communicate effectively with communities across Asia and the world.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: In this regard, we have provided more opportunities for our students to use the Malay Language beyond the classroom.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: This programme promotes the teaching and learning of the Malay Language for preschoolers, their parents, and teachers through fun-filled activities at the Singapore Zoo.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: So, they will learn the Malay Language when they visit the Singapore Zoo.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: We will continually review our efforts to make language learning more authentic by leveraging on creative methods so that the love for Malay Language will continue to blossom in the hearts of our students.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: (In English): In conclusion, as we enhance our education policies in response to changing needs, we will help every student make the best of these opportunities and nurture them into skilful and resilient Singaporeans.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: We must also work together to strengthen the inclusiveness of our education system, so that no one is denied of a good education because of their circumstances.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I accept the Minister's arguments that the PSLE could, in fact, offer an important checkpoint and allow parental choice with regard to secondary school entry.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But I wonder if he would not also agree that allowing a parent to choose for their child not to take the PSLE is yet another dimension of choice.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: If so, then what are the inhibitions behind the – and I will emphasise this word – "optional" through-train policy as the Workers' Party (WP) has proposed?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Does it have to do with resource constraints, such as a belief that it is not possible to create such through-train schools?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Or is it more with a perceived lack of demand, as he may have alluded to?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: If it is the latter, what then would be the hurdles to piloting this for just a small number of schools to gauge the take-up?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Mr Chair, I thank Member Assoc Prof Jamus Lim for allowing me to elaborate on this.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But let us just walk through the process, and we have thought about this.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Should we pilot a few schools for through-train?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So let me walk through the process and some of the things that we have to step through in order for us to consider this.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: If the through-train programme is to a very popular school – and you know which one I am talking about – I am sure there is no shortage of takers for this through-train programme.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But what about those who develop a bit later and want the chance to go to some of these schools?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Does it mean therefore they do not get the chance to go to these schools?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And how does that affect the social mixing that we spoke so much about in this House?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Who gets to go through a through-train programme?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The second issue: supposing, I, as a parent, I decided that my child will go for the through-train programme.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Sometime during primary school, I figured out that my child may not be suitable for this programme.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This then might consequently mean the fourth issue, which is that in a secondary school, every secondary school which is in the through-train programme must be able to cater to the diversity of learners.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We are not ideologically closed to all good ideas.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I have also spoken with my foreign counterparts.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, I would say this: we have considered this and we are still considering this.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We have to step through the issues, non-trivial issues, systematically.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, I repeat what I mentioned in my speech.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But let us get the reasons right – why do we want to remove or want to consider removing the PSLE?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Let us not do it for the wrong reasons and let us not end up with unintended consequences.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: First of all, regarding Full Subject-Based Banding (FSBB), it is heartening to hear Minister Maliki mention that students will have multiple options to take, especially in the polytechnics, from FSBB.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But I have a question which is a different side of the same coin.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Conversely, will some students perhaps be restricted in their options after they have finished secondary school?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: So, for example, if I had taken Chemistry or Maths before and I just managed to pass, then I could maybe take it still in junior college.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With FSBB, if I took Chemistry or Maths at a G1 level, would I still be allowed to take it?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Or would it be because I did not take it at a higher level and therefore the pathways are restricted for me if I did not take a subject at a sufficiently high enough level at G2 or G3?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I think Minister Chan mentioned that it is good that we can access SLS anytime anywhere.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As a parent of a child in Primary 6, I must say that it is a very, very useful system indeed.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But while we can access it anytime anywhere, Minister, what about those students who may not have the devices to access it?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Are there schemes or plans to ensure that students have the device, whether it is a tablet, a mobile phone, or even a laptop, to ensure they can fully reap the rich benefits of a system like SLS?

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: First, I think we want to ensure that we understand and parents understand the concept and philosophy behind FSBB.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: It is really to recognise the potential of every student with regards to different subjects.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: Traditionally, we assume that you do all the subjects in the same level.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: That is where the streaming came in: the Express, the Normal (Academic) and the Normal (Technical) streams.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: But we acknowledge that over the years we want to facilitate students' ability to focus on subjects that they are strong in and also do subjects that they may not be strong in but are capable of coping with.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: And so, when we look at the post-secondary pathways, it is really to recognise that and how we can find the combination.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: So, the question is, when you are doing G1 today, where do you go afterwards?

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: In the FSBB programme, it is what we call the education and career guidance; career guidance by the teachers to help the students at each level.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: So, at Secondary 1 when you come in after PSLE, you are guided in terms of your performance at PSLE.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: And looking at your strengths in each subject, the school and the teachers will guide the students on what they can and should take when they get into Secondary 1.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: And then by the time they get to Secondary 3, as they prepare for the major examinations, they look at the performance again.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: So, there are expanded pathways and this allows them to feel that they are not  pigeonholed at such an early age.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: That has been the feedback from many Members of the House that we should not pigeonhole our students too early but instead allow them to explore their own potential.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: I hope that that flexibility allows the students to also feel good, and that the revision of the education system is really meant for them to grow and appreciate their own strengths.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: All our secondary school students have their own personal learning devices.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Any primary school students who require a device because of their family circumstances can approach the school for help.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: But I would like to first clarify that in my proposal for naturalistic pedagogy, it is not so much of asking MOE to do more but an invitation to MOE to consider "how else might we"?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: So, I would like to ask Minister whether MOE might be open to make a pathway of teacher training in naturalistic pedagogy possible for the new cohorts of teacher-applicants at NIE to explore this pathway.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: And the second question is related to this; I heard the Ministers' encouragement to our companies and the private sector, we are constantly encouraging the private sector to hire based on skills and not qualifications.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We thank Ms Carrie Tan for her suggestions.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We understand the spirit of what she is asking.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Whether naturalist pedagogy will be in the mainstream pathways, I will have to leave it to my professional colleagues in NIE to make the judgement.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But we are always open to explore all the different pedagogies, whether to adapt and adopt them in part or in full, to benefit our students.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Second, technically, I should not be answering this because the Member asked why the industry is not recruiting people based on currency rather than grades?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Well, as the former Minister for Trade and Industry, maybe let me hazard a reply.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I think all of us are human beings, including HR professionals.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We sometimes fall into the habit of trying to reduce everything into something that we can manage.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, in the past, maybe we were all very comfortable with reducing the perception of ability to a single unitary dimension, which is called either the GPA or the grades.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But having said that, as the former Minister of Trade and Industry, I have seen many progressive companies that have actually gone beyond this, and I have always encouraged my teachers to go and visit some of these companies to understand their HR processes.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: In fact, last year during MOE's annual workplan, I asked one of my teachers this question: do they know what will be the first question that the potential employer will ask our students?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: To be fair, not all my teachers will be familiar with this because they are not in the business.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, I encouraged them to talk to the employers.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And I also encourage the employers to come and talk to the schools to help our students understand the kind of abilities and capabilities required for the future.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The second thing that I think we can do to help us evolve faster in our mindset is this: we have to invite all the industry leaders to come into our schools to see our students, be it ITE, polytechnics or even secondary schools.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And, in fact, some other countries can just call their polytechnics "colleges" overnight and award "degrees".

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Our polytechnic students are not any worse off compared to many of the foreign graduates.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, go beyond the title of a diploma or a degree and look at the actual skill sets.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: When the industry people come and join us on the boards of the schools or the ITEs and the polytechnics, and whatever they feel that we are not doing adequately, give us the feedback, we adjust the curriculum and we will have a faster speed to market timing to help the industry fulfill their manpower needs and, at the same time, allowing our graduates from our polytechnics, ITE and universities to be much more industry-ready.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, I think we need to work hand-in-hand, but we need to go beyond this mindset and reduce all the abilities of the individual to one matrix.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And the last appeal that I have, when I speak to all my industry partners, is this: MOE will never be able to produce the perfect student and perfect worker for you with all the requisite skills because it does not exist.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: As the MOE students join you to become the workers in the industry, it is also the responsibilities of the industry to keep training our students and to keep them up to date.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Otherwise, there is no way that we can produce that perfect student that meets all the industries' needs forever.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: In fact, I did a thought experiment with a group of entrepreneurs whom I met.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I said, "Why don't you tell me all the skill sets that you want from our students?" So, they gave me a long list of all the skill sets that they desired.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: As the former MTI Minister, why don't I make you a deal?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I will produce the students with all these attributes in five years' time, in 10 years' time and you sign me a contract that you will employ them when they graduate." None of them took up my offer.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Because they realise that whatever they say today will be outdated by then and in MOE, we are in the lifelong education business.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We cannot produce people with skill sets	overnight.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We want to make sure that we are still top of the league as they grow older.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: I have two clarifications for Minister of State Gan Siow Huang.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: It is related to the speech I made.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The first clarification is, Minister of State actually responded to my call that from the vast group of SkillsFuture training providers, it is time for the Government to streamline into three categories and actually, indeed, that is the plan.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Could Minister of State elaborate on the criteria that MOE will be using to streamline the whole group of 790 training providers which I counted online?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The second recommendation I gave to Minister of State is about the idea of appointing lead training providers for each of the key sectors along the Industry Transformation Map (ITM).

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: A little bit about the idea like anchor operators in the childcare sector.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: You work closely, they are selected by the industry and, most importantly, they must be set up to do practice-based training, not just academic but to reskill people with practice-based curriculum using real-life simulation.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: People who teach those programmes are industry leaders so that the skills are really practice-based.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: So, can the Minister of State comment on that?

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Before I answer that question, I just would like to add to what Minister Chan said in response to Ms Carrie Tan's question about why there seems to be companies who are hiring based on qualifications instead of skills, despite it being common sense that actually it is more sensible and logical for employers and HR to hire people based on skills.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: In my interactions with companies as well as with our training providers, I understand that some of our companies, especially the smaller ones, may themselves not be very clear about the definition of skills.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: And it is very useful for companies that need help in identifying the skills for the different job roles in their companies to refer to the skills framework.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: This will help them in better defining and hiring people based on their needs and not to over-hire.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: For example, it is quite common that I hear from Workforce Skills Qualifications (WSQ) sometimes in job advertisements, companies put out an ad that they want to hire an undergraduate in ICT.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: But actually, could they have considered a diploma graduate in ICT?

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: How familiar are they about the differences in the skills that our university students and our polytechnic students have in terms of ICT?

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: There is also responsibility on MOE's part to help employers out there to understand the differentiation and we will do better in this.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We also hope that through work-study programmes and apprenticeship, employers will be able to better understand, see and experience for themselves the quality of our students, whether they are from ITE, polytechnics or universities, and not just blindly assume that they are of certain differences in standards based on qualifications alone.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We also look at employment outcomes for people who are already being hired or already have a job.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: But going through the training, they are able to qualify for a higher job role.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: That, we deem to be a tangible employment outcome.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: So, those companies and training providers that provide such courses, we will want to provide more funding support basically, to lower the costs of these courses and also to steer more trainees into these courses provided by such training providers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: But we also know that it is not always so easy for a person to get a promotion straight after attending a course or to land a job immediately after completing a programme.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Sometimes, it takes multiple steps before a person can land a job or get a promotion.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: So, we do track this overtime and we look to our industry partners, trade associations and looking forward to NTUC, the unions as well that commit a lot of their resources and the unions' workers for training, to give us the feedback so that SSG and the Government can, through multiple sources of information, be able to better identify training providers and courses that can make an impact on the workers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: On the other question where the Member mentioned anchor operators – yesterday, Ms Foo Mee Har also brought up the concept of a lead training provider, I believe.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: These are what I would deem to be equivalent or similar to the concept that Ms Foo Mee Har is referring to.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We have them in retail, tourism, hospitality and so on.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: They are the ones that we deem to have reached a certain high level of standards in training and generation of workers for the industry.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Many of them are industry leaders themselves, not necessarily training providers, or pure training providers or IHLs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We do look for training providers that are strong in producing trainees of good outcomes.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Just as I was about to ask that Members keep their clarifications short, I think, it would be fair, if the response could be also a little bit shorter.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I just have two quick clarifications for Minister Chan in relation to the P1 registration framework.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I fully agree with Minister's view that we need to change mindsets here.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: And so, for the first clarification, in terms of the societal circumstances and needs which Minister spoke about before making further changes, can he elaborate further on what these are?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: And second, in relation to that, I understand alumni ties and community ties – not meant to be literal – are important to parents.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: But, at the same time, could we not then look at the home-school distance as a primary factor while still keeping some of these other ties in relation to the secondary critieria, to send the right signal that distance and convenience for their children would be the most important factor?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: First, when the country was young, community-based groups and alumni, they all played an important part, and they still do in helping to foster a sense of community and spirit.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But as society matures, there is always a risk that such groups become closed and exclusive groups.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: That is why, over time, we must find that balance.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: That is what I mean by societal circumstances.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, if we accept that there is a role, a need for some local community, we also accept that home-school distance is important for the convenience of the students and the parents, and once we accept that there are these two, sometimes competing considerations, then our job is to find the balance.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And we must be prepared to adjust the balance according to circumstances and the societal needs.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: In fact, if we only use home-school distance alone, then we may have another unintended consequence, which has happened in Singapore and elsewhere.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: What happens is that, for the so-called perceived popular schools, everybody will want to move near there; and now, instead of competing at two kilometres, it may be one kilometre or 500 metres.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, it does not really solve our problem.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Somewhere in Boston, once upon a time, there was one particular school that nobody wanted to go to because it was up and far away from central Boston.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, all the immigrants went there because it was far away.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And after many years, the hardworking and talented immigrants all made a name for the school.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And lo and behold, every well-endowed family started moving to that school.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Today, that school is a very good school in Boston, with a very well-heeled community around them.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Have they solved the problem of diversifying the base?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: With all good intentions, it was defeated by human preferences.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: If we think that that is far-fetched, I suggest that it also happens in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I just like to ask the Minister regarding SLS that Minister shared earlier.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I laud the efforts by MOE to push towards digitalisation and EdTech.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: My question is in regard to accessing SLS and the Minister mentioned, accessing it from anywhere.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: My concern is, as I go around to meet my residents, I see some of the students at home with their grandparents, some are in broken families.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: My question is whether SLS will be data intensive?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And when it is data intensive, what type of extra help can we put in place together with the other Ministries to make sure that some of these students can be helped, especially in terms of data costs and access to SLS, which is exceptional?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Chairman, the short answer is that this is something that we have already done, during the COVID-19 times.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: During the COVID-19 times, we did two things, which Members may not be aware of.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Minister, I think the "no PSLE through-train" idea was not just a Workers' Party (WP) idea.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: And I know that the MOE staff had gone through the idea, even during Deputy Prime Minister Heng Swee Keat's time.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The second clarification is about MOE Kindergartens (MKs).

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I know that when MOE first entered this space, it was to give access to the less advantaged or disadvantaged preschoolers.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Second is also to learn a little bit more about the space of early childhood education, in terms of content,  pedagogy and assessment.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: So, I want to ask what lessons has MOE has learnt from this MK initiative?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: And how can they be shared, to ensure that those who have no access to these good MKs have a chance to also learn and everybody can be uplifted, in terms of early childhood, preschool or kindergarten education?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: My third one is: I know that, as some of the Members, including the Minister, have mentioned,  quite a number of employers are still fixated on paper 	qualifications versus skills as the proxy for promotions and for hiring.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I know it is not easy, but I wonder if the public sector, being the biggest employer in Singapore, can show and lead the way?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: There are some jobs that are probably being done already in the public sector that use skills-based instead of paper-based criteria.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I also know, however, that in education or in a non-profit organisation, one of the conditions is that there must be some kind of paper qualification.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And that is through the Direct School Admission (DSA) system, where they can use different abilities to get into different schools that specialises in different areas.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This is slightly different from a through-train because it is not one-to-one.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: It is one based on merit to your specific skills.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And FSBB will continue to expand this to reduce the stress, if stress is the concern.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But as I mentioned, stress cannot be the only reason for us to think about this.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: It must be how we can better make use of the time for the holistic development of our children.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Second, Ms Denise Phua asked about the MK lessons.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I worked on this with Deputy Prime Minister Heng Swee Keat when I was the then-Minister for Social and Family Development and he was the then-Minister for Education, that we started MK for a couple of reasons.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: First, at that point in time, there was a plethora of pedagogies and practices across all our preschools, and we wanted to make sure that we have a body of knowledge that we can set as our baseline.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The third comment by Ms Denise Phua, I will make sure that the Minister-in-charge of Public Service gets the message, and we will continue to do that.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: So that you also do not have to second-guess the other schools and try to get the other schools' papers and stuff like that.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: That would also lighten the load of teachers – by setting examinations for subjects at the cluster level.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Chairman, we thank Mr Patrick Tay for his suggestion.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Indeed, that is something that we have considered very seriously in MOE.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And I will say a few things in response to that.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The baseline is 80%; do as much as we can to share, to lighten the workload and for the remaining 20%, you must customise.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The second comment that I would say is that: yes, indeed, we appreciate the Member's affirmation of our teachers.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: When it comes to FSBB for the same subject, the teachers may have to set three different sets of paper because of the three different standards.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, indeed, it is a lot of work.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But I must say this: our teachers are not afraid of hard work; they just want the work to be meaningful so that they can help our students to grow and grow well.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The third thing I would caution in this idea is that, while we try to harmonise the examination papers by region, as the Member said, we are careful not to turn this into a mini-PSLE at different levels, at different regions, because then, you have to coordinate everybody coming to take the paper at roughly the same time.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But I do not think the intent, and I do not think that it is your suggestion to turn it into a mini regional PSLE system.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, there will be some differentiation in the test matrix across the different schools, to cater to the different needs.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But, indeed, we want our teachers to share more.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: So, the Minister mentioned about the Teacher Growth Model (TGM) and for anything to grow, we need space.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: So, a suggestion, and I want to follow up on the suggestion by Singapore Teacher's Union (STU) with regard to the white space for teachers.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: They would like white space where they can do their things, their marking and their counselling for students, because right now, while they do have space in between their lessons, it is really for them to rest and to eat.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: So, I was wondering if this could be part of MOE's consideration.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: And second is with regard to the flexible pathways for our IHL students, I am glad that we have these flexible pathways for them, but at the same time, more flexible pathways and giving them extra modules to take means they need more time.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Would the Ministry be considering that they might need more time and they might need longer to finish the programmes?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Mr Chairman, let me answer Dr Wan Rizal's with a more nuanced position.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We agree that we want to give more white space to our teachers.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But our definition of white space is a bit different.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: It is not so much for you to just rest, do counselling, do marking and prepare lessons.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: That, to us is part of the work; it is not really white space.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: They can go for teachers' work attachment class, gain experience, exposures and networks beyond the school system, so that they can grow personally.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I have always said this to all my teachers: when I visit all the schools – I visit one or two schools every week – I do not have to look at the students first.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I just need to look at the teachers.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: If the teachers are tired, the students will be tired.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: If the teachers have the sparkle in their eyes, the students will have the sparkle in their eyes.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: That is why I keep saying: as our teachers pour their hearts out to take care of our children, it is our job to make sure that we take care of our teachers.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Respect them, give them time and space to grow.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: ITE College West is situated in my constituency, so I have a first-hand encounter on how the ITE students have organised activities for my Choa Chu Kang residents very well.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: And these students are supported by very caring ITE lecturers, who not only teach, but also care for them, as many of these students come from disadvantaged families.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Therefore, can MOE consider giving ITE the flexibility to employ more teaching assistants to augment the lecturers?

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: Chairman, I thank Mr Don Wee for his questions.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: It is very heartening when you hear Members of the House asking for more resources for our teachers and expressing their full support and empathy for the challenges that our teachers experience.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: In particular, for the ITEs, we know that ITE do have students who are coming from challenging backgrounds including SEN students.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: This is also in line with Dr Wan Rizal's question earlier about the flexibility that we are giving our students in terms of the way they cope with the curriculum.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: We do want them to go through at their own pace albeit looking at the structures we have in place, but certainly, support will and continue to be given to all our students as well as our lecturers and teachers.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: So, the diverse pathway is really about allowing the students to know where they are, understanding their family circumstances and we will support them along the way.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: With regards to the additional support, yes, given the additional challenges and learner profiles that our ITE has, we are working with the ITE to augment them with more resources.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: We do know some of the students do come from very challenging backgrounds.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: Our lecturers, just like our general education teachers, go on home visits, knock on the doors, find out where they are and try to bring them back to school because that is really the passion and desire of our teachers to make sure that our students complete their education.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: So, I want to assure Mr Don Wee that we are augmenting our ITEs with resources required for them to support our students and given the flexibility that we are introducing, we will certainly work together with them to make sure that this will not unduly pressurise the teachers, but rather inspire them further that what they are doing is very much supported by Members of the House, by the community and certainly, we will support them in every endeavour that they embark on in supporting our students.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Chair, I promised Mr Patrick Tay, his Iron Man.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The other day at an environmental event for schools, I was also told that the Minister for Education could be like Captain America, to save or change the world by shaping the next generation.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Be it Iron Man or Captain America, we all have great expectations of MOE and perhaps, also for the Minister for Education, to do wonders for the world.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And some of you might have arrived at the conclusion that MOE is a very powerful Ministry, as we do move property prices and determine traffic jams at the Causeway.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But on that day, I told the audience that I do not aspire to be Captain America.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Or even Captain Singapore, as some drew a parallel to the initials of my name.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I say I would rather be a Catalyst Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The difference is this: the future cannot and will not be shaped by the superhuman capabilities of one man or woman.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I do not think you can, nor should it be the case.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Instead, if MOE can catalyse and ignite the power of every Singaporean, we will be more powerful than any superhero.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: All Singaporeans can be given the opportunity to be superheroes.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I hope those who can will also have the gumption to do so.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Where everyone defines success not by our achievements but more importantly, by our contributions where we each understand our own strengths and weaknesses, even as superheroes, play as a team, win as a team.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Where those with great powers exercise greater responsibilities to help those with less, those who are little and those who are lost.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Where we define success, not by how well we do for ourselves in this generation, but more importantly, how we enable the next generation to do even better than us in this generation.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: With your partnership, I fear not, that we cannot.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Let our next generation be the superheroes that they want and can be.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And one final point, Mr Chair, I understand that Parliament does not allow or encourage the display of any partisan symbols in this House.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But I noticed that today, Speaker and one of our Members have probably displayed product placement on your chest.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Some like Mr Speaker will certainly say that for our education system, "The Best Is Yet To Be." I say, "The rest also can be".

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Together, we move towards the "better age" and "forge a better life".

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But we must always remember to "lead with passion, serve with compassion".

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And finally, to Deputy Prime Minister and Mr Patrick Tay, especially for you, "Nothing Without Labour".

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Special thanks to our Government Parliamentary Committee (GPC) Chair.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Patrick Tay, would you like to withdraw your amendment and end the class, please?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: I will end off with my school's motto, "Potest Qui Vult" – "If there is a will, there is a way".

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: On that note, thank you very much and I beg leave to withdraw my amendment.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The past few years have undoubtedly been a test of mettle.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Especially so for our educators and school staff who have worked tirelessly to ensure our students are safe and schools remained open during the pandemic, all while balancing their own demands and caregiving needs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Not to forget the staff in MOE headquarters who have toiled in the background, coordinating and supporting our schools' responses.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I tip my hat to all of you for taking every challenge in your stride as you continued steadfastly to mould the future of our nation.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: With business and economic disruptions occurring at a more rapid pace, identifying the skills demanded in the future and equipping our learners with these in a timely manner will be a perennial challenge.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: COVID-19 showed us how quickly our modes of working can be upheaved but it also showed us that if we can react rapidly, we can seize opportunities even in challenging times.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: As our education system evolves, I hope that we do not just do more, but do better.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Our mainstream school students have access to education and career guidance throughout their education journey, all the way up to their time in Institutes of Higher Learning (IHLs).

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: However, once they leave the IHLs, they may no longer have access to subsidised professional career coaches, which is unfortunate.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Coaches work with us to explore our strengths and weaknesses, build confidence and chart our career paths.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: They are invaluable resources throughout our careers and the start of our career journey should be no exception.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We owe it to our youth, especially those who have given up much during the pandemic years, to help them get a strong footing on the career ladder.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Understandably, our IHLs, or what Minister endearly calls Institutions of Continuous Learning (ICLs) may want to concentrate their resources on current students.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: By the same token, only the unemployed and retrenched have access to employability and career advisory as supported by Ministry of Manpower.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I hope that the Government will consider allowing youths as well as workers in general to make use of their SkillsFuture credit for career coaching services, since this aligns with its aim which is to encourage individuals to take ownership of their skills development and lifelong learning.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This will also mitigate against skills, jobs and expectations mismatch which is a cause of our structural unemployment problem here in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The next area we can do better in is access to quality CET and to make CET a way of life.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: If we think about it, CET is very similar to Iron Man's Mark suits.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: On his own, Tony Stark is human, though a brilliant and resourceful one.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: But when he puts on his Mark suits, he becomes Iron Man, Earth's Best Defender.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Similarly, when adult learners participate in CETs, we upskill and reskill ourselves, allowing us to respond constantly to evolving industry needs and challenges.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Just as Tony Stark upgrades his Mark suits to prepare for future and more lethal attacks, we upgrade our skills and employability with each CET qualification obtained, improving our chances to bullet-proof ourselves against curve balls and seize opportunities in the future economy.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Thus, I urge MOE to dedicate more and latest resources into encouraging and catalysing both employer-supported and individual-initiated training so that we can weather any storm and fight new challenges.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: And just as Tony Stark is selective about the modifications that he makes to his suits, we must also ensure that the CET offered are well-designed to attract adult learners who have to balance work and other commitments.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: CETs must be relevant to the demands of industries or they will not be effective at improving employment outcomes.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: CET providers and industry must collaborate closely so that our CET offerings can be adjusted in response to rapidly changing needs of our economy.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: NTUC is more than happy to support this collaboration via our network of unions and company training committees.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: But even the best Mark suits are of no use if no one wants to put them on.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We must help Singaporeans recognise and embrace lifelong learning as a continuous process.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Through school, we build strong foundations; through work, we gain practical experience; and through CET, we stay up-to-date and remain competitive.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Mainstream education, CET providers and industries must work together to develop curricula and programmes that would equip learners with skills and knowledge they need to succeed now and in the future.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This will help our learners realise the value of ongoing personal and professional development and industries to have access to a highly skilled and capable workforce.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Singapore's system of meritocracy has been debated many times.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: While it encourages us to strive for better outcomes, it has led to an endless paper chase as degrees and diplomas are used as proxies for individuals' skills.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: But these papers only reflect skills at a particular point in the learner's life cycle and are not the be-all and end-all.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Employers need to recognise that the mark of a high-performing individual is in his skills and competencies.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Mindset shifts will take time especially when it comes to deeply ingrained beliefs and habits.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Together, these will encourage lifelong learning and enable learners to take ownership of their own career development.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Chairman, education is very close to my heart.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I made almost 30 speeches in this House on education, including on schools for the future, removing the PSLE, through-train schools, tuition, special education and lifelong learning.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I will touch briefly on the future of education today.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: These five key strategic shifts include moving education from the first 15 to the next 50 years, harnessing strengths of the whole of society in education and other strategic moves.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: But as we know, behind every big vision are thousands of plodding steps needed to make the vision a reality.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: There are not only current structures, systems and processes but also current mindsets to reckon with.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Many of the required key shifts articulated by Minister Chan sound like the proverbial new wine that needs to be stored into wineskins.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: We have heard of how one does not pour new wine into old wineskins, lest the new wine will burst the old wineskins and both wine and skins are destroyed, lost.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: So, would the Minister please share his analysis of what might be the driving and restraining forces of making these key shifts, the new wine, in education and what needs to be done to secure a good future for Singapore's education system?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: As long as most businesses and schools do not have an effective alternate system of assessing competencies and proficiencies, the focus on the traditional exams and academics will continue.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Seriously study the potential of through-train schools without the PSLE, micro schools – with school sizes of say 100 to 300 students, quality home schools and lifelong learning schools especially for students with disabilities who are unlikely to be well-served by the mainstream SkillsFuture offerings.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The use of approaches such as the individualised education plans, blended pedagogy, technology and harnessing the whole of society can similarly be applied and quality need not be compromised.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Now, much has been spoken of the success of Singapore's 15-year-olds in PISA, the OECD’s Programme for International Student Assessment.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: However, not much is said of the Programme for the International Assessment for Adult Competencies (PIAAC) or the OECD Survey of Adult Skills.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: So, as lifespan and retirement age rises, more aggressive steps are needed to uplift this segment of at-risk Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: So, in conclusion, Sir, for our education to be relevant and ready for the future, we must identify and work on the game changers to significantly move the needle.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: If any country can do it, I believe Singapore can.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Mr Chairman, more private preschools are increasingly incorporating nature and outdoor-based learning for children.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Besides better physical development, it also helps children improve mental well-being and develop higher intuitive intelligence.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: This refers to the ability to think holistically, to think paradoxically, to listen and connect to oneself and others and the ability to lead by influence rather than design.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: As the world evolves with new climate realities, we cannot be playing catch-up in preparing our young for future jobs in the Green Economy.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: It is imperative that we equip our young to be "nature natives" and not just "digital natives".

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Beyond occasional visits to farms and community gardens, children in preschool and kindergartens can be introduced to the sciences by playing in nature and be guided to observe how plants, animals and other elements in nature interact in symbiotic relationships.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: They can learn spelling by identifying plants and creatures, be taught teamwork collaboration through play-based lessons and fun projects in the outdoors.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: In lower primary, students can learn conventional subjects like science, mathematics, commerce and communication through nature-based approaches such as tending to food gardens and harvesting produce to be sold in a school cooperatives or other enterprise or social projects.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Upper primary students can be facilitated to learn organising skills, collaboration and leadership by leading these projects.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Real world application-based learning from a young age will help an increasingly evolved and questioning generation to see relevance in their education.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: This can segue into the International Baccalaureate (IB), General Certificate of Education (GCE) or Institute of Technical Education (ITE) options depending on the inclinations and aptitude of the youth.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Parents can voluntarily sign up if they are keen to give their children an alternative approach to education.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: This will ensure that the transformation of our education system is evidence-based and at a measured pace in partnership with parents.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Mr Chairman, first of all, I declare that I run a company operating education centres and a private school.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There should be no sacred cows in education.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The learner, especially the well-being of the child, comes first.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Another sacred cow to slay is the size of our schools.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There is no "one-size-fits-all" solution in school size policies.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In our international school scene, families may choose from a variety of schools that best fit their children's profiles.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There are primary schools that take in less than 200 students to big schools with a few thousand strong student population.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For local students, we only offer big schools.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: MOE merges schools because of falling birth rates and changing demographics of housing estates.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I urge MOE to consider a range of school sizes for the sake of our changing learning demographics too.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We want to move towards inclusive learning where neurotypical and neurodivergent children play and study well together.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Small schools have the advantage of developing deeper connections between staff and students.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Just being able to know everyone by name can build a stable, safe environment for children who feel left out and whose needs go unaddressed in big spaces and also, big class sizes.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Lastly, I want to bring up the Student Initiated Learning (SIL) programme.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Last year in October, MOE in response to my question, replied that SIL is "time is set aside for students to pursue their own interests and learn outside the curriculum.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is to encourage students to be more curious and self-directed in their learning" and that "Preliminary feedback indicate that SIL is valued by schools and students".

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The feedback that I have received on the ground is that the reception to SIL is uneven.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, I do hear of instances where students who are not keen on the scheme choose to "learn" things that they already know.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As this is a new initiative with an approach quite different from what is traditional in our schools, teething problems are of course to be expected.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Do not let them feel this is just another programme imposed on them from above.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Making this programme optional will also allow us to get a more accurate picture of the level of acceptance.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And whilst our teachers and students take time to get used to the idea of student-initiated learning and how it can benefit them, perhaps schools can offer some structured programmes that students have voted for as mid-way measures?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Another suggestion is to allow students to use Medisave to learn from classes at SkillsFuture and related online courses.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Let us help students build a customised, relevant skills-based portfolio.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They can match their learning interests from any class and vendor around the world.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Although I personally dislike taking tests – and as an educator, I lean toward minimizing the use of quizzes and exams – I am actually pretty decent at them.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: My wife, for all her innate talent and creativity, and bless her heart, turns out to be pretty bad at them.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Yet tests are a common feature in the education landscape, both here and around the world, and most of us endure them, for good or ill.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The ubiquity of tests and the varied performance of otherwise, like comparably-talented individuals, has resulted in an active debate about the value of high-stakes, standardised tests.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: One important reason for such variability – and for anyone who has experienced that stomach-churning sensation come testing time – is that test anxiety is real, can negatively affect performance and is unrelated to actual ability.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Another is that individual motivation differs when confronted with the prospect of a test and this motivation is only weakly associated with performance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Indeed, when COVID-19 struck, a host of universities chose to suspend testing as a requirement for entry and have chosen to retain this practice even after the pandemic.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This list includes august institutions, such as Amherst, Brown, Cornell, the University of Chicago, Harvard, Stanford, WashU in St Louis, Williams and Yale.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: All this has led to a re-examination of the merits of high-stakes tests.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Diane Ravitch, an education policy analyst that once was an advocate of testing and who oversaw the development of such tests in US schools, now call for an abandonment of standardised testing.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The evidence aside, the reality is that a reliance on grades and test results are becoming less and less critical in many important settings.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: When I was in graduate school, it was common knowledge that those who excelled in the coursework component of the programme would not necessarily go on to become the best researchers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The top student in our first year dropped out in our second, to become an actuary, rather than see through the rest of the PhD programme.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In contrast, one of our other mates, who had failed several of our first-year comprehensive exams, eventually went on to graduate, is now a practicing economist at a central bank and routinely publishes papers in academic journals.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Beyond academia, more and more companies are eschewing formal traditional test-based metrics.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Google famously does not hire on the basis of grades and no longer even requires a college degree, preferring to evaluate applicants on the basis of actual work produced.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Thus, their first major examination will be at secondary 4.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Children develop at different rates and this option allows certain kids to learn at a pace that is more suited for them.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Importantly, offering the extra room for children to blossom and to reach their full potential before they turn 16 could actually be even more important than allowing them to skip a major test at the age of 16.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Certain schools already have a variation of 10 YTS.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This proposal merely suggests an extension of the programme to a different high-stakes standardised test.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Students who wish to continue taking the PSLE may still do so.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Perhaps more critically, this proposal does not mean that frequent teacher feedback, in the form of other feedback via other than high-stakes standardised testing should be de-emphasized.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In fact, there is solid evidence that such feedback, along with other practices such as increased instructional time and specialized tutoring, is what distinguishes effective schools from those that are less effective.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The key is not the frequency by which tests are administered, but rather to treat the interaction between teacher and student as an interactive, ongoing dialogue.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Chairman, full Subject-based Banding (SBB) introduced in 2020 is an important element of the goal of MOE to instill in students a love of learning.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: An extension of MOE's 2018's SBB, it allows students to take the English Language, Mathematics, Science and Mother Tongue languages at a more demanding level at secondary 1, based on their performance in these subjects at the PSLE.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: From 2020 to 2024, the full SBB has been introduced to allow students to learn each subject at a level suited to their strengths, interests and learning needs.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This move is also the result of positive feedback from students and parents, I believe, and teachers as well, and also indicators from the O and N-Level examinations.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With the full SBB, I believe that the Express and Normal Academic streaming has been ended.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Instead, students will be in mixed form classes, allowing them to engage with peers with various interests, aptitude and strengths.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This will also open multiple pathways for students based on their aptitudes and interests.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Can MOE provide updates on the progress of SBB?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What are some of the challenges faced in SBB?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Is there a plan to enhance the programme and perhaps offer other subjects in the future?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Baey Yam Keng, you can take your two cuts together.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: It recognises that each of us could have a different attitude towards different subjects.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: These allow students to learn at a pace and level according to their academic abilities in specific subjects rather than their overall academic performance.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: More importantly, it will help our students nurture the joy of learning.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: MOE has taken a careful and measured approach in rolling out this programme.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Indeed, it should be so, as we must be sure of the benefits of any change in policy.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Different bands may require different teaching resources such as textbooks, laboratory equipment and teaching staff, which may be difficult to provide for all students in each band.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Compared to the past when students stay within their own class for all subjects, full SBB means that students could have different classmates for different subjects.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: While these will allow students to learn with different schoolmates and make more friends, it could have an impact on the forging of a form class spirit.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: After we graduate, we tend to have class gatherings, now students might need to have gatherings by subject band classes, or would they not even feel close enough with their classmates in different band classes.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: I feel that a dilution or even loss of affinity towards a class would be a sad consequence of full SBB.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Therefore, may I know what MOE has observed about our students' school experience under full SBB?

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: When students are used to be able to study different subjects at different bands, they will need to follow through in terms of similar flexibility in learning and accessibility to more pathways and learning opportunities to the post-secondary education.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: I know that for A-Level subjects that we have offered at H1, H2 or even H3 levels.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: I would appreciate if the Ministry could share any plan in this area.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: With easy access to the wealth of information on the Internet and availability of Artificial Intelligence (AI) like ChatGPT, education has to go beyond acquisition of knowledge.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: We have to learn how to find information, process information, turn the information into knowledge and learn how to apply the knowledge.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Our students need a wide range of 21st century skills and competencies to thrive in a complex and fast-changing world of today.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: I am glad that MOE has been progressive in its education philosophies.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: I believe this has been very much welcomed by students but perhaps only by some parents.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: This is when I urge parents to support MOE in this and fill up the freed up time and space that the kids have with more tuition and enrichment.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Will we be able to relieve some of the examination preparation and stresses?

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: The "A" Level system has been the traditional academic pathway post-secondary school for majority of students who are aiming for university education.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Over the last two decades, however, there have been many options that have emerged: speciality schools, Integrated Programme (IP) through train programme, International Baccalaureate (IB) and the polytechnic courses have also become more attractive and diverse.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: I believe that tweaks have been made to the "A" Levels over the years in 2007 under the revised curriculum.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Students were allowed to select subjects from three levels, Higher 1 (H1), Higher 2 (H2) and Higher 3 (H3).

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Subjects are divided into knowledge skills and content-based subjects.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Knowledge skills subjects include General Paper (GP), Knowledge and Inquiry and Project Work and content-based subjects divided into languages, Humanities and the arts, and Mathematics and Science.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Under MOE's regulations, students sitting for the "A" Levels in a junior college (JC) are required to take at least one subject that is from a contrasting discipline.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: These are indeed moves in the right direction.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: My question is: can MOE share if the "A" Levels are still relevant in today's education landscape and how it would compare to other post-secondary qualifications, such as the IB and even polytechnic diploma in terms of admissions to our Singapore universities?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: At this point, I would like to declare my interest in an enterprise in the education space in markets including Singapore.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In order for our schools and universities to thrive, they must be mindful to make themselves accessible to students from a wide variety of backgrounds.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Top universities, like the Ivy League and Oxbridge universities often make their admissions statistics widely available and publish targets on increasing access to admit more students from vulnerable or lower-income backgrounds.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The careers services of such universities also often heavily emphasise and rely on alumni to maintain guidance for students and former students who have since graduated.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Indeed, I was myself involved in being a student mentor at my university, providing mentorship for promising sixth formers, or "A" Levels students, who would be the first in their family to attend university.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I also continue to occasionally receive emails from current or recent students of the university, seeking careers advice on topics relating to different career pathways and options.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It is with this in mind that we managed to successfully launch a mentorship programme for students in Sengkang two years ago and many of our participants found it helpful to be able to discuss their educational and career options with mentors from a wide variety of backgrounds.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I am happy to see more constituencies outside Sengkang starting to roll out mentorship programmes.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This would also make it easier for our fellow Singaporeans to measure the success of and thus understand moves, such as relocating popular schools out of central Singapore, in an effort to be more inclusive.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We could also move to have our alumni more heavily involved in advising current or even prospective students into our popular schools and IHLs, not because there is a benefit to be gained, but because they wish to genuinely share the benefit of their life experience with younger fellow Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Moving on to enrichment programmes, it is true that MOE, the Ministry of Social and Family Development (MSF) and other agencies are working towards increasing access to tuition.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While a good start, these programmes typically focus on more academic programmes, and leave students from lower-income families still unable to attend robotics or AI classes, forest school, for example, and other types of holiday camps which have proven to be equally if not more beneficial for children's holistic development.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This would be especially important in today's fast-changing environment, where the ability to pass examinations is only part of a measure of life success.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We also need to think outside of the box and go beyond the traditional smaller scale tutoring system.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Instead, their child was posted to a primary school that is several kilometres away from their home.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: This has caused them great inconvenience as the child would have to take public transport or wake up very early in the morning to take the school bus to the primary school which the child was posted to.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Sometimes, the school may not have a school bus connection to the child's home.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Hence, these parents appealed for their child to be admitted to a school that is nearer to their home.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Young children should not have to wake up too early and travel a longer distance than necessary to their school.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I urge MOE to review the Primary 1 admission scheme.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The younger students will then get more rest at home and this will reduce the need for the school to arrange for school transport for the pupils and reduce worries that a bus operator may not perform the expectation as we saw recently in St Stephen's School.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In his Budget speech, Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong spoke about building a fairer and more inclusive society.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This allows more children who have no family connections to the school to get admitted into a school near their home.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: But I believe the changes do not go far enough.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Why are we still entrenching the mindset that just because my father or mother went to a certain school and so did I; hence, I must get my son or my daughter into the same school as well.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Minister Chan's reply was that MOE needs to avoid causing disruptions to parents and take care not to drastically affect the groups given priority under the current framework.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: But if inherited parental privilege is protected at the expense of another child being turned away from a school that is only a few hundred metres away from their home, can we truly say that our system is fair for all?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In the past, MOE has been constrained by a need to respect the history and legacy of many schools which started off as community initiatives.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: But the impending move of ACS (Primary) to Tengah and the largely positive response is drawn from parents and alumni tells me that attitudes are shifting.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Muhamad Faisal Abdul Manap, you can take your two cuts, please.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: This is because of the full-time madrasahs' status as a private education institution and not a public school.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: This was the reply given when I asked in 2015.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: At this point, I would like to declare that I have a child who attends full-time madrasah.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: What I would like to propose is for MUIS is to continue giving awards, but only for religious subject as they are a statutory board which regulates Islamic education system in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: My suggestion is meant not just to boost financial support for our madrasah students and their family.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: It is also meant to foster a greater sense of solidarity amongst all our students regardless of whether they are attending madrasah or Government school.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
