text: This will, in turn, add to our existing efforts to maintain inter-religious, and inter-racial harmony in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: MOE's Financial Assistance Scheme (FAS) aims to provide financial support to Singapore students, from the low-income households studying in the public schools or public-funded schools.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Were parents choose to enrol their child in a full-time madrasah, it is to aspire the child to be equipped with both academic and religious knowledge.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Our public schools do not provide the latter.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I note that MUIS does provide financial assistance in the form of Progress Fund Madrasah Scheme (PROMAS).

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I have come across cases of low-income Singaporeans parents who has a child or stepchild who is a Permanent Resident and are struggling in their child's education expenses.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Some even ended up with school fees arrears, even though they are paying subsidised fees.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: A good number of these Singaporean parents had attempted to acquire Singapore citizenship for their child or stepchild, hoping to alleviate the financial cost.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I note that between 2019 to 2021, around 30% to 40% of all marriages involving Singaporean citizens were transnational marriages.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Some of these marriages do lead to children who may not have Singapore citizenship.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Chairman, as an educator, I have seen first-hand how students' mental states can impact their learning engagement and ability to achieve their full potential.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Students today face a unique set of challenges unlike those faced by few years generations.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Rapid technological advancements, economic uncertainty and a dynamic job landscape are just a few examples of the challenges our students must navigate today.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Students also deal with increasingly complex, social and personal pressures that impact their well-being.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: For example, social media have fundamentally changed how students interact with each other and the world around them.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: While social media can be a powerful tool for communication and self-expression, it can also create an environment of constant comparison and pressure to present a perfect image of oneself.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This can lead to feelings of anxiety, low self-esteem and depression among youths.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: In light of these challenges, we need to work towards identifying areas for improvement and develop more relevant and effective strategies to support our students' well-being.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Mr Chairman, recent reforms such as the new PSLE scoring system, the introduction of some aptitude-based admissions and the removal of mid-year examinations are commendable steps to make education more equitable, holistic and less exam-focused.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: However, we should ask what more we can do to reduce unhealthy competitive stress in schools.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: To address the fact that better-off children can access better private tuition and enrichment classes, MOE should facilitate the production of engaging and easily accessible educational materials that are freely available online to students such as podcasts and explainer videos.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: For example, according to the 2014 publication, Regulating Private Tutoring for Public Good, from the University of Hong Kong, South Korea's educational broadcasting system was established in 1990, with high-quality radio and television programmes, including, since 2004, lessons to prepare for standardised university entrance exams.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I have come across the perception in some quarters that students from better-off families have better access to internships due to their parents' networks.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This is where MOE can come in to better improve the link between companies looking for internships and those less popular post-secondary and secondary schools who can offer interns.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Spending time as an intern, imbibing work cultures and norms, helps divert some mental energy away from the excessive focus on academics.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It is certainly something that has been appreciated by my residents.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It is a great example of how we can give a headstart for Normal (Academic) students who are traditionally seem as being behind the Express cohorts.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It has taken away stress and opened doors, giving them flexibility to choose a pathway that is based on their aptitudes and interests.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Indeed, the flexibility provided by the PFP would ideally be in a future of full subject-based banding, pervasive in the system rather than a special scheme.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Can the Minister provide and update on how admission pathways to various post-secondary education institutions will be updated in line with the shift to full subject-based banding to make it easy for all students to develop to the best of their potential?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: Chairman, the job landscape is dynamic and evolves rapidly and job requirements are changing along with it.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: When you consider external constraints like the pandemic, jobs can become redundant or evolve altogether.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: Thus, there is a need for us to have a flexible curriculum that develops our students with a wide range of skills and helps them pursue their passion outside their main areas of study.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: In my Budget speech recently, I mentioned that Jobs-Skills Integrators scheme is a gamechanger because they will change the mindset that skills training can translate into good employment outcomes.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: I hope we can embed it in our ITEs and polytechnics, where students can stack skill modules on top of their specialised course.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: It may increase their employment opportunities and allow them to remain agile in a dynamic job space.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: My greatest hope is that it will also address the issue of increasing income wage gap between the non-graduates and the graduates.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Chairman, COVID-19 was a painful and challenging experience, but it did provide opportunities too.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Technological developments in education and corresponding education technology (EdTech) had to be accelerated due to the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Digital technologies and the use of technologies to enhance and supplement conventional learning became much more prevalent.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Students and teachers had to quickly pivot to home-based learning (HBL) when the COVID-19 pandemic struck in 2020 and the switch to digital learning platforms has indeed gained strength.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Even as face-to-face lessons have continued now, teachers have pivoted to online learning to supplement face-to-face lessons.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: The use of tools like Kahoot, Mentimeter and Slido for quizzes and polls and virtual bulletin boards such as Padlet are some examples of how teachers and educators are harnessing technology for interactive and responsive learning.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: It adopts a responsive agile approach and structure to help MOE respond rapidly to technological and contextual changes to ensure the effective use of EdTech for quality teaching and learning.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Besides tech to enhance and support learning, tech advancements like ChatGPT will also impact teaching and learning too.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: The Minster for Education addressed the issue of AI and ChatGPT at a recent Parliamentary Sitting, but I would like to ask if MOE could give an update as to what it learnt from the experience of the COVID-19 pandemic in terms of EdTech and how EdTech can be harnessed and used to enhance the teaching and learning journey.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Also, how will we be retraining and upskilling our educators in tech and preparing students and parents for these changes as well.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: I wish to repeat the call to MOE this year.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: With more technological advances, it is easier to do research over the Internet and secure the answers to most queries.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: The need to acquire so much knowledge is really no longer necessary because most information is easily available on the Internet.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: What a student needs to learn is how to navigate the Internet so that he is able to obtain reliable and accurate information.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: The advent of ChatGPT will also change the way students learn.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: In a Straits Times article just last week, Google was reported to say that one of the most valuable qualities that they look for in an employee is a "growth mindset".

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: Google did not say they were looking for people with great academic grades or people who know everything.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: Google said they were looking for people who express curiosity – for people who continue to learn.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: The Straits Times article was not about a high flying employee who was a scholar but about a user experience engineer without a degree.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: This will then cut down the stress from projects, continual assessments and exams.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: A reduction in school curriculum and exams or assessments would reduce the stress on today's students.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: Schools shifted to home-based learning, highlighting the need for a robust technology infrastructure and content-ready digital resources to support teaching and learning.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: As technology continues to advance rapidly, it has become increasingly important to integrate it into teaching and learning practices to prepare students in the modern world.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: In the Parliament recently, I asked the Minister about the use of AI tools like ChatGPT.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: I started out having some resistance of my own, but having seen the capability, I am encouraged that it can help students.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: Sure, you will not get an A or B grade, but if it can give a student who is struggling, to give them that nudge to a C or a pass, to get them to open a book or their notes and cross-check the AI solution for content accuracy, then I say, let us do it.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: The world is changing at an unprecedented rate and our students will be facing challenges and opportunities that were not even imagined a few years ago.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: The pace of technological innovation, the rise of automation, the impact of climate change and the increasing interconnectedness of the global economy are just a few examples of the complex issues that our students will need to navigate as they move into adulthood.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: To prepare our students for this complex world, we need to focus on building their resilience and adaptability as well as their skills and knowledge.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: This means not only providing a strong academic foundation but also fostering their creativity, critical thinking and problem-solving abilities.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: It also means equipping them with the social and emotional skills that are essential for success in life.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: These include self-awareness, self-management, social awareness, relationship skills and responsible decision-making.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: These skills will help our students to develop strong and positive relationships and to navigate the challenges and opportunities of the complex world that lies ahead.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: We are certain that we will require a partnership framework to augment the school system.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: As such, how can we build partnerships with parents, the industry and the wider community to nurture resilient and holistic students who can thrive in a complex future?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Students with higher needs, including those from disadvantaged backgrounds, require more support to ensure that they have an equal opportunity to succeed.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: There are a number of reasons why this is the case.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Students from disadvantaged backgrounds are more likely to face barriers to learning such as challenging family circumstances, access to learning resources as well as proper nutrition.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: These barriers can make it more difficult for them to engage in school and achieve their potential.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Students with higher needs may require additional support to overcome specific challenges such as learning disabilities or mental health issues.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Without this support, they may struggle to keep up with their peers and may become disengaged from the learning process.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: They simply need a better learning environment, more opportunities and time.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Providing support for students with higher needs is not only a matter of inclusive values of the education system but also an economic imperative.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Studies have shown that students who receive additional support are more likely to complete their education, to go on to further studies or employment and to make a positive contribution to society.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: It is essential that we provide more support for students with higher needs, including those from disadvantaged backgrounds.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: This may involve additional resources such as funding, extra staff, equipment as well as targeted interventions that are specifically tailored to the needs of individual students.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: As such, how are we better support our students with higher needs and those from disadvantaged circumstances?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Persons with disabilities (PwDs) need access to training and lifelong learning just as much as their able-bodied counterparts.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, they sometimes face access barriers to attending courses.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Accessibility should be embedded in all SkillsFuture-funded courses.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: There should be a set of guidelines to ensure that reasonable accommodations are provided.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: MOE could also establish a disability support office to provide support to PwDs and training providers to implement reasonable accommodations for SkillsFuture courses.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I appreciate that SG Enable is curating courses suitable for the disability community and the Enabling Academy will assist in creating accessible courses.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, to be fully inclusive, PwDs need access to all courses which are open to the general public, not just a curated subset.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I have shared my experiences and journey with my son, Ayden, several times in Parliament.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: My family and I have been truly blessed with the support of many people in the ecosystem.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We have also learnt a lot from the people who have walked the journey before us.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Their experiences and feedback over the years have helped create awareness and shape the support structure that we now have for our children with special needs.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This will of course always have to be a work-in-progress.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: There should be continuous efforts to enhance the support in the ecosystem.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It is imperative that our education system adequately equips all our children, including those with SEN, with the necessary life skills and prepare them for future challenges.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Integration is an important element as we should teach our children to learn and interact with people with different abilities.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: All our children are unique and they should grow up appreciating and respecting each other’s strengths and value they bring to society.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: However, in integrating students with SEN with the rest of the community, we should do some calibration as there may be a tension between creating the common spaces and learning opportunities while at the same time paying sufficient attention to the additional support and teaching that needs to happen to build the skills of those with SEN.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: There may be a great desire to be inclusive but this may bring SEN students into a setting that does not necessarily empower them or equip them with the skills or address their needs.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: They may be put in the same classroom and there may be some additional support to help them with that particular assignment or activity.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: But is the curriculum for them robust enough to build their own skills to be independent?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: How are they interacting with other students and how are other students interacting with them?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: How are we assessing their abilities to subsequently navigate living in the larger community?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: How do we ensure that we are adequately stretching them to reach their full potential?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: These are some considerations that I hope that the Ministry is looking into and could give some insights on.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: For the larger community, there is always a forward-looking agenda, one that looks at growth sectors and economic opportunities and a curation of existing educational or skill-building pathways that prepares us for the future.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: There should be a similar approach for our students with SEN.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I appreciate that there are diverse needs among students with SEN.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Are we looking at the current jobs that the different groups of SEN students are landing and their career progression?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I am hoping with these insights, we could then better develop our curriculum to ensure our SEN students can be channeled into meaningful sectors where they can grow and contribute like everyone else.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Lastly, I would like to revisit a point I made in Parliament previously.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: An integral part of all the efforts in integration, in building appropriate skills is the special needs educators.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We need to ensure we have professional, good and skilled teachers in schools specialising in special educational needs so that we can translate the vision into reality.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This will encourage more individuals to come forward to be part of the workforce and hopefully, create a larger pool of capable educators who can look into more specific issues and enhance the support for our students with special educational needs.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The points I have raised above are not new.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: With the increasing awareness and more people coming forward to be part of this cause, I believe it is a good opportunity for us rethink our efforts in enhancing the education for our children with SEN and ensure they are able to integrate with the larger community.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: During one of a meeting I attended, Ms Denise Phua said something that stuck with me.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I am paraphrasing a little but she said, “let us ensure that as we are developing our plans in preparing our workforce and our people for the future economy and future challenges, we think about those with special needs and they are not just a footnote or an after thought”.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I acknowledge that work ahead is not easy but it is important and needs to be done.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I have been encouraged by the efforts of the Ministry and other agencies and I hope that we can continue on the vision of preparing all our children for what is to come and moulding the future of our nation.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: Beyond social integration, many of them also need a diet of additional lessons in life skills such as work habit development, communications and social skills.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: The rest, 20% of students with SEN, are educated in some 20 Special Education (SPED) Schools.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: Many exit at the age of 18 unless they are assessed to be capable of getting a work skills certificate.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: For students with SEN in mainstream schools, I urge the MOE to: One, put aside resources to study and analyse the educational outcomes of SEN students in mainstream schools in primary, secondary and post-secondary school settings.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: Two, develop an assessment framework to regularly evaluate if the current intervention approach is providing each SEN student the holistic education that they need.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: Three, adopt a holistic individual education plan for each mainstream student with SEN, covering not just their academics but also other indicators of student well-being.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: Four, tap on expertise in the SPED system to systematically address the gaps not covered in the mainstream set up.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: The current criteria for staying till age 21 is based on whether one can stay on to get a work skills certification.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: SPED students need longer learning runways to build vocational and other life skills for survival especially in this rapidly fast-paced and wired world.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: Two, jointly work out and pilot a lifelong learning SPED school model with a taskforce of thinkers cum doers with a track record to create a school like no other in the world.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: And three, support SPED schools in specific areas of need.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: Review salaries to attract and retain good staff.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: Expand the pool of potential SPED educators by allowing MOE NIE candidates to apply to join SPED schools.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: Keep to very essential and core admin reports and meetings so that educators and school leaders can focus on educating their students.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: I urge MOE to continue to expand its vision to meet the lifelong learning needs of this special community so they will thrive and not be left behind.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: Teaching can be challenging yet rewarding but also requires much physical, emotional and mental energy.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: Sometimes it may lead to stress and even burnout.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: Together with STU, I have a few suggestions.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: One way is the introduction of a whitespace for marking, lesson planning and student guidance or counselling work.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: Second, could the Ministry cultivate teacher agency so teachers can negotiate deployment to achieve win-win outcomes for the teacher and the school?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: The teacher agency could also help teachers plan for their re-employment years so that they make purposeful decisions in keeping with their life stage and priorities.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: Notwithstanding the questions posed earlier, could the Minister share MOE’s plan to support the growth and well-being of teachers?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Chairman, industries are now skills-focused and appreciate usable skills over paper qualifications.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Industries value students who acquire the skills in school and are ready to be productive when they join the workforce.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: With the rapid evolution of technology, there is a need for schools to be well connected to the industry and nimble enough to make frequent tweaks to the syllabus such that students leave school with the right skillset required for the industry at that point of time.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I am heartened to see more schools having career days, where they invite people from the industry to share their experience and the skill sets that are required in the industry.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Individual ITEs have also reached out to industry partners to try to understand industry better such as ITE College Central's engagement with the aerospace industry, just to name one.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Beyond individual school effort, how can MOE better facilitate collaborations between schools and industry partners to help students in our schools gain an even deeper appreciation of the skills and competencies needed in the future workplace?

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Chairman, I am a director and shareholder of various private education institutions and I consider myself privileged to be part of the stellar education system that Singapore boasts.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: As we all know, Singapore is home to some of the world's best universities.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Our public school system is among the world’s best and our students consistently scoring near the top in education rankings in OECD countries.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: But our local and international schools offer a wide range of curricula which provide quality and holistic learning experiences aimed at equipping students with the necessary skills for the future workforce, and our excellent tertiary institutions and research facilities make Singapore an ideal place to pursue higher education and participate in innovative research initiatives.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Our global reputation for academic excellence is not the only reason why Singapore is one of the top destinations for international students looking to pursue high quality education.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: There are at least three other reasons why Singapore has grown to be the academic hub that it is.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: First, Singapore has excellent transport links with many other countries, which makes it easy for international students to travel to and from their home countries.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Second, we have a highly developed and efficient system of infrastructure and public services, which make for a high quality of life for its residents.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: And third, the promotion of English as the primary language spoken in Singapore means that international students can easily integrate into the country without having to learn a new language.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: In the same vein, the significance of international students cannot be understated.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: They bring diversity and cultural richness to Singapore's society.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Additionally, with the influx of students from different countries, these educational institutions provide an invaluable opportunity for cross-cultural exchange and collaboration.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Furthermore, international students can help expand the global reach of Singapore's private education sector, increasing the international visibility as a leader in high quality education.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Chairman, private education institutions (PEIs) have a vital role to play in Singapore's success as an education hub.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: These institutions offer Singaporean students the chance to pursue specialised vocational diplomas or degrees from foreign universities whilst in Singapore as an alternative to attending our local universities.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: PEIs can also provide tailored curriculums adapted to a student's specific needs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: I wish to suggest that the Ministry consider funding a network of international schools located in all major regional capitals within ASEAN.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: These schools will offer the full Singapore curriculum similar to that of any local MOE school, from the kindergarten through to the secondary school level.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Students that attend such schools would be able to transfer relatively seamlessly from a school back in, say, Jakarta or Bangkok, back to one in Jurong or Buangkok.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: They would pay comparable supplemental fees just as any student enrolled in a local school would.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: And they would take the same common exams – PSLE, “O” or “N” Levels – at the appropriate time and level.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Why would the taxpayer wish to subsidise schools located in other countries?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: For starters, students attending these schools would be Singaporeans more likely than not.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: It makes sense that they be provided with a subsidised Singaporean education as others in their cohort are.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Moreover, these children are often simply following their parents overseas as they are being posted rather than making any conscious decision of their own to relocate.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Furthermore, the subsidy has an additional benefit from the perspective of the parents.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: By reducing the frictions associated with moving their families to a different country, it offers positive incentives for our local professionals to relocate and thereby upgrade their experience and exposure to the region, which is often cited as a reason for local middle managers being skipped over for promotion.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: So, there is already a precedent to this suggestion.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: She also mentioned, however, that there was a lack of demand for such education elsewhere, which was why it was not offered beyond Hong Kong.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: To this, I will only add two thoughts.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: First, it strikes me as unusual that Singaporeans living in Hong Kong, an otherwise modern and sophisticated educational system, would demand more Singapore-style education there rather than in other ASEAN capitals with comparatively weaker educational systems.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Second, such demand itself is, in fact, endogenous.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: If such schools existed, it would encourage more locals to consider taking on regional postings, which in turn would generate the requisite demand.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Through Enterprise Singapore, the Government is expending much treasure to support our firms in their regionalisation efforts.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: It has also worked hard to encourage our professionals to consider regional postings.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: What I am suggesting here today is simply another step towards lowering the barriers to making our local talent ever more international and ever more competitive.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: I spoke during the debate on the Budget Statement of how reskilling programmes are critical to building resiliency in our workforce and our people as the economy and job market become more unpredictable.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: It has been several years now since we laid down the importance of lifelong learning in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: Support is now more geared towards getting adult learners into new jobs and the range of courses supported has also been refined.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: Identifying the right set of skills to offer courses for is important, but there are many factors that influence the attitudes of and persistence to succeed for adult learners – from structural factors like range, availability and delivery methods of the courses, including pre- and post-employment support, as well as environmental factors such as a growth mindset, family and financial responsibilities and time constraints.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: What are the metrics and where do we stand?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: How will the Government continue to evolve its support to develop resilient adult learners?

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: Chairman, the Skills Demand for the Future Economy (SDFE) Report 2022 highlights the importance of upskilling workers to stay relevant and take on new opportunities.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: IHLs, private education institutions and other training providers play important roles in developing and curating training courses to respond to this need, especially in terms of sustainability skill sets for Government officers, industry leaders, practitioners and other stakeholders.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: As demand for subsidised for SkillsFuture-funded programmes continues to grow, it can put increasing strains on training providers.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: Is the Government considering streamlining SkillsFuture Singapore processes to ease the administrative burden on training providers?

speaker: Mr Mark Chay
text: Mr Chairman, I am a director and shareholder of various private education institutions and I have had some experience with the Skills Framework, which is designed to provide key information on sectors, career pathways, occupations or job roles, and existing and emerging skills required for the occupations or job roles.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay
text: It helps provide critical information on the general career pathway, the roles within these sectors and the skills required to meet those roles.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay
text: The Skills Framework is a masterpiece that took great effort by the relevant stakeholders such as the employers, Government agencies, trade associations and so on to assemble.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay
text: It is therefore pertinent to ensure that the framework is reviewed and updated from time to time to ensure that this remains in step with applicable and emerging trends and developments.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay
text: A critical piece for the success of continuing education is access to courses, namely, through Approved Training Organisations (ATOs) and Private Education Institutions (PEIs).

speaker: Mr Mark Chay
text: Currently, two different regimes govern private training institutions in Singapore – the ATO framework and the Enhanced Registration Framework (ERF) for PEIs.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay
text: Under the ERF, certain PEIs who meet high-quality assurance standards would also be granted the "EduTrust" mark.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay
text: For instance, can the process be streamlined so PEIs with EduTrust qualifications qualify to become an ATO?

speaker: Mr Mark Chay
text: I understand that currently, all IHLs are exempted from such checks and can offer SSG/WSQ courses without having to qualify under the ATO framework separately.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Chairman, I would like to declare my interest as the CEO of the Wealth Management Institute, a training provider serving the finance sector.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: There has been much scrutiny on the effectiveness of SkillsFuture in achieving its mission of supporting workers to upskill, build deep capabilities as well as transition to new careers or different industries.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: These courses are delivered by a large number of over 790 training providers ranging from large autonomous universities such as NUS to private training organisations of varying size and focus.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Given the sheer volume of training programmes and players involved, it is hard to ascertain the training impact of all the programmes under the SkillsFuture umbrella.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Category A: for programmes that would be designed to support jobseekers' reskilling needs, matched to industry talent demands.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Therefore, these programmes are likely to be intensive and need to be purposefully designed to be effective.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Category B programmes would be about upskilling and building mastery amongst practicing professionals and craftsmen, an important part of continuing education and training for working adults.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Category C programmes support skills discovery, including the learning of new hobbies and interests, many of which can be supported through the People's Association community platform.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The requirements on the rigour of the programmes should also vary according to the learning objectives of the programmes.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: For example, for category A programmes, courses would have to be full-fledged certified programmes that lead to verifiable credentials recognised by the industry.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: These programmes should be organised along Industry Transformation Maps and be subjected to a rigorous assurance process by relevant industry panels and associations to ensure relevance.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The teaching faculty should come primarily from the industry to impart highly practice-based skills, using work-related simulations and practices as well as internships as core components of the training programme.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Job placement should be a key performance indicator.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Most importantly, trainees who gain admission to these category A programmes and successfully graduate should be sought after by future employers as they are deemed to possess the necessary skills and competencies required of the new role, having gone through the training.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: It is currently based on training subsidies provided to trainees.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: This system incentivises the training providers to maximise student numbers and not the quality of the training.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Furthermore, as training subsidies can change from time to time, impacting demand, sometimes, in short notice, training providers find it challenging to invest in their programmes as they are unsure of their future income stream.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Let us call them lead training providers (LTPs) for each of the industry groups.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: LTPs should be chosen by the industry and serve as the respective industries' centre of excellence for training and education so that scalable training may be delivered to meet the manpower needs of the respective sectors dynamically.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: These LTPs should be eligible for substantially more funding support for developing their infrastructure and industry relevant programmes.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: At the same time, they should be subjected to a vigorous governance and review process by SkillsFuture Singapore.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: The Industry Transformation Map provides a high level overview of what are the skills that are required in industries.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: However, when it comes to applying in on the ground, potential jobseekers are overwhelmed.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: They are overwhelmed by what courses to take to find better jobs or be better at their jobs.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: While we unanimously agree that upskilling and retraining will be critical to our future success, the challenge is how do our jobseekers upskill and how do we then match jobseekers with their newly acquired skill set to vacancies?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: How can MOE strengthen the training and placement programme, particularly in the fragmented sectors, to better match jobseekers' skills to vacancies?

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Mr Chairman, SkillsFuture is a national initiative in Singapore that aims to equip Singaporeans with the necessary skills to succeed in a fast-changing economy as it prepares Singaporeans through a comprehension scheme involving elements such as the SkillsFuture Credit, the SkillsFuture Work-Study Programmes, SkillsFuture Series courses.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: The SkillsFuture series courses are available at an affordable cost and provide individuals with the opportunity to acquire new skills and knowledge quickly.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: However, course fees are only one determiner of the success of these courses in training adult learners.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: While we equip them with skills, can the Government also do more to help ensure that they are able to translate this new training and skills into actual jobs?

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Also, specific groups of workers may also face peculiar challenges when upgrading.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: There could be sectors that require particular attention.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: How can older workers be helped to upskill while continuing to work?

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Mr Chairman, Singaporeans will need greater agility and resilience in learning, amidst the rapid pace of industry transformation and more dynamic demand for skills Several Members including Mr Darryl David and Ms Mariam Jaafar asked how we will enable workers to adapt quickly to the changing job environment.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: The SkillsFuture movement is our national effort to build a culture of lifelong learning and equip Singaporeans with the skills they need to adapt and thrive.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: It requires ownership by employers, individual learners, and training providers, as well as close partnership of the tripartite partners.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: In my speech, I will outline how we are supporting companies, individuals and training providers to be a part of this collective movement to secure our future.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Over the years, more companies are stepping forward to train and develop our workforce, lending strength to our SkillsFuture movement.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: For FY2022, SSG estimated that about one-third of its total expenditure on training support would go towards employer-sponsored training.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: To ensure relevance and responsiveness of upskilling, we will continue to work closely with companies as a key partner in workforce development.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Workplace Learning, in particular, is a key strategy that we are pursuing as it allows workers to upskill in-situ and on the job, minimising operational disruption to companies and workers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Since 2018, the National Centre of Excellence for Workplace Learning (NACE) has been helping companies to systematically build workplace learning capabilities.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: This year, NACE will partner NTUC to pilot the Workplace Skills Recognition (WPSR) Programme.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: First, NACE will introduce a new tier of workplace learning certification, the Workplace Learning: READY (WPL:READY) mark, to recognise companies with basic capabilities in workplace learning.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: NACE, NTUC and SSG will reach out to SMEs to equip them with capabilities to analyse their training needs, develop plans and processes to support workplace learning, and most importantly, train and recognise the competencies of their workers in specific skills.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Second, for SMEs that have attained the WPL:READY mark, NACE and NTUC will work with them to fast track the assessment and recognition of skills that the workers have acquired at the workplace.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Workers in these SMEs can attain WSQ certification without having to attend external WSQ courses, once they are assessed to have acquired the necessary skills on the job.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Workers and employers in the Progressive Wage Model (PWM) sectors can benefit significantly from such an initiative.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: SSG and NTUC will start this pilot with SMEs in two PWM sectors – retail and food services.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Under the PWM, a Retail Assistant needs seven skills in order to take on the role of a Senior Retail Assistant.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Today, these skills can be acquired through WSQ training programmes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: With Workplace Skills Recognition, the Retail Assistant who is working in a WPL:Ready mark company could be trained and assessed in these skills on the job.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: They can also be given the appropriate WSQ certifications for the skills that they have demonstrated at their workplace.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: The certifications will enable the Retail Assistant to qualify for future promotion to the Senior Retail Assistant role under the PWM framework.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Through this pilot, we hope that companies will be able to sustain upskilling of more workers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Mr Patrick Tay suggested that employers provide training leave for their workers to undergo skills training.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We will consult our tripartite partners and study the idea of training leave further, taking into account and consideration the impact on businesses, especially SMEs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Besides supporting individual companies in upskilling their workers, we also want to help companies appreciate the broader shifts at the industry level and the impact on them.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: The Industry Transformation Maps (ITMs) set out roadmaps for 23 industries, integrating restructuring efforts between the Government and various industry stakeholders.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: All 23 ITMs have been refreshed, with updated jobs and skills strategies, to respond to a post-COVID-19 world.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: In addition to the ITMs, companies can also reference SSG's Skills Demand for the Future Economy Report published in November last year.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Using big data, the report provides an update on key developments and trends in the Green Economy, the Digital Economy, and the Care Economy, as well as changes in the skills that are needed across industries.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: I strongly encourage employers to take a look at the report if they are thinking about the new skills that their workers might need.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We will need to do more at the industry-level to coordinate training and placement efforts in sectors that are less regulated and have more SMEs, as mentioned by Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong in the Budget speech.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We will appoint suitable intermediaries such as industry associations, employment agencies and institutes of higher learning (IHLs) as JSITs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: NYP has a Centre for Digital and Precision Engineering, which has been playing a key role in training students and adult learners, for the PE sector.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Over the years, it has established strong partnerships with various training providers, as well as industry stakeholders.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: The PE sector has a high concentration of SMEs as well as mature workers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: The sector is also known to have jobs and vacancies that are quite hard to fill.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: At the same time, industry transformation in this sector requires some employees to move into new roles in the future.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: As the JSIT for the PE sector, NYP will engage companies to understand their manpower and skills needs and review existing training programmes to meet the needs of the industry.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: NYP will partner the Singapore Precision Engineering and Technology Association (SPETA) to engage companies in the association's network.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: NYP will also work with employment agencies and other training providers to enhance placement support and training for companies in the sector.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: For SMEs in the PE sector that find it challenging to track industry developments, articulate your skills needs to training providers and find workers with the right skills, NYP can serve as your first port of call for advice on emerging skills needs and industry-relevant training programmes for your workers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: You can benefit from new manpower pipelines, with trained and skilled workers who can meet the demands of hard-to-fill or newly created jobs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: For workers in the PE sector, NYP will work with partners to offer careers and skills advisory services and industry-relevant training programmes to support you in your career development.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: For jobseekers, NYP can connect you with employment agencies and potential employers who can provide more information about the PE sector.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: You can access industry-relevant training programmes and employment facilitation services that are curated by NYP to support you in your journey.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Through this pilot, we hope to better meet the industry's need for skilled workforce, while enabling more workers to take up upskilling to meet their career aspirations and to stay employable.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Last year, about 560,000 individuals participated in SSG-supported programmes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: This is a higher number than the pre-COVID-19-pandemic level.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Mr Patrick Tay suggested allowing individuals to use their SkillsFuture Credit for career coaching services.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Mr Darryl David asked how we ensure individuals who undergo reskilling and upgrading will be able to find jobs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: During the pandemic, SSG ramped up train-and-place programmes, which combine skills training with employment facilitation to help individuals move into new industries or job roles that are relevant to their training.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: The outcomes for these programmes have been encouraging.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Since last year, the SkillsFuture Career Transition Programme (SCTP) was introduced to help train and place mid-career workers into new job roles.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Apart from facilitated training, the programme provides career advisory and employment assistance to support mid-career workers in their job search.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: SSG provides baseline subsidy of up to 70% of the course fees, and enhanced subsidy of up to 90% of course fees for Singaporeans aged 40 and above.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: This will provide significant support for mature workers which Ms Denise Phua spoke about.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Ms Ong Choon Mei, a former financial advisor, who successfully switched to the HR sector, is an SCTP beneficiary.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Taking a career break to explore other opportunities last year, she enrolled in the SCTP in Applied HR and Business Digitalisation, a four-month course conducted by Singapore Polytechnic.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: As at December 2022, we have successfully launched 82 SCTP courses, in 10 sectors with good employment opportunities, including infocomm and technology, professional services, and healthcare.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: From April to December 2022, there have been over 1,000 enrolments.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: A vibrant, high quality and market-responsive training and adult education (TAE) sector is key to the success of the SkillsFuture movement and lifelong learning in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: The types of programmes we fund and the outcomes we tie our funding to, are important levers for us to achieve this.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Ms Foo Mee Har suggested introducing a quality framework that would require us streamlining courses and grouping them into three broad categories with distinct objectives, including funding allocation and key performance indicators (KPIs).

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Her suggestion reflects our current plan to a very large extent, as SSG has started its transition towards outcomes-based funding.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: These courses include full qualification programmes and stackable modules that are recognised by the industry.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: SSG will continue to provide subsidies at up to 50% of the course fees for standalone courses that are designed to provide just-in-time, bite-sized skills top-up.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: These includes the SkillsFuture Series courses that are aim at developing emerging skills.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: To foster a culture of lifelong learning, individuals can continue to use their SkillsFuture Credit for these courses.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Across all three categories, SSG will track the quality and outcomes through audits, and by seeking learner and employer feedback.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: SSG will do more to enhance the quality of the feedback and to share this with individuals, so that they can make informed choices.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: But we will also need the involvement of learners and companies to close the feedback loop with us and improve the system for all.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Beyond its funding framework, SSG also looks at developing capabilities in the Training and Adult Education (TAE) sector.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: In 2018, SSG developed the TAE Industry Transformation Map (TAE ITM), in consultation with industry and training providers, to drive innovation and enhance productivity in the sector.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: One of the priorities under the refreshed ITM is to raise the industry relevance and market responsiveness of training.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: The Skills Frameworks, which Mr Mark Chay asked about, facilitate this by providing critical information on sector transformation and a common skills language for workers, employers and the training providers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: A previous survey conducted on around 1,900 companies found that 44% had adopted the skills frameworks.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: The skills frameworks have been especially useful in our Progressive Wage Model (PWM) efforts.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: SSG is also driving innovation and digitalisation of the TAE sector.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Prof Koh Lian Pin asked whether we could reduce the administrative burden on training providers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Indeed, as part of TAE ITM, SSG will continue to do so by promoting process digitalisation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: For example, SSG is now replacing manual attendance-taking processes with e-attendance taking via Singpass.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Mr Gerald Giam asked about how SSG ensures that SSG-funded courses are accessible to persons with disabilities (PwDs).

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: As far as is practicable, training providers will admit PwD learners into existing courses by making necessary adjustments.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: SSG is working with SG Enable under the Ministry of Social and Family Development (MSF) and other stakeholders, such as Social Service Agencies (SSA) to further expand CET opportunities for PwDs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: This includes providing grants for training providers to customise courses for them.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We appreciate that PwDs have very varied learning needs and training providers assess them, on a case-by-case basis, to provide customised training support.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: As a percentage of Gross Domestic Product (GDP), our spending is comparable to the other Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) countries and we continue to grow our investment in this area.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Several Members asked about the outcomes that the SkillsFuture movement has achieved.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Having invested significantly in this, what have our efforts led to?

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Wage and employment outcomes are the most tangible and concrete measurable outcomes arising from skills training.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We monitor these outcomes through programme-specific surveys and studies.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Their median salaries were also higher than what they received at the start of the programme.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: In 2019, the Ministry of Trade and Industry (MTI) published a study showing positive effects of the Singapore Workforce Skills Qualification (WSQ) training on labour force participation and wages in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: However, wage and employment outcomes do not always tell us the full picture.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Reskilling may have helped workers, who were otherwise at risk of displacement, to keep their jobs or to move to new roles.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: These positive outcomes might not show up if we only looked at wages and job placements.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: This is why we should take a broader view of the impact of the SkillsFuture movement and signpost progress over time.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: One dimension is whether the training helps workers to be more effective.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: In the Training Quality and Outcome Measurement, or TRAQOM, survey that SSG conducts on the courses it supports, more than nine in 10 trainees said that the training enabled them to perform better at work.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We will continue to assist companies in developing workers and support individuals in their upskilling journey.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Importantly, we must have a continuing, active conversation across different stakeholders on the skills that are needed, which types of training are helpful and impactful, and where the gaps might be.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Strengthening the impact of the SkillsFuture movement is a collective effort, and we must join hands on it to succeed.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Mr Chairman, allow me to say a few words in Mandarin.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: (In Mandarin):   Workplace learning is a key area of support for businesses.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: The National Centre of Excellence for Workplace Learning (NACE) will work with NTUC to help SMEs strengthen their workplace learning capabilities and certify their employees' skills.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Employees can obtain accreditation without enrolling in designated courses.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: The programme will first be launched for SMEs in the Retail and Food Services sectors.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We must also enhance coordination in employee training and employment.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Nanyang Polytechnic will engage businesses to understand their manpower and skills needs, and work with training providers to ensure that trainees are equipped with the skills needed by the industry.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: The JSIT will also work with employment agencies to strengthen employment assistance for job seekers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: (In English): Let me now respond to cuts filed by Members on other topics and give an update on MOE's Green Plan.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Mr Mark Chay asked about MOE's plans to improve the quality and credibility of private education institutions (PEIs), and whether applications for student passes and other approvals can be more seamless.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: MOE and SSG regularly review the Government's standards required of PEIs under the mandatory Enhanced Registration Framework (ERF) and EduTrust schemes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: The onus, though, is on PEIs to regularly review their curricula and course offerings to ensure that they prepare their graduates well.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: This is a one-stop process and most applicants are notified of the outcome within one month.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Mr Mark Chay also asked whether different registration processes can be streamlined.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: PEIs are educational institutions that offer programmes, such as diplomas and degrees which students may invest substantial time and money in.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: The ERF ensures that PEIs have baseline standards in areas, such as corporate and academic governance, with a focus on consumer protection, while the EduTrust scheme further distinguishes PEIs with a consistently high standard of governance.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: The registration of training providers for their causes to be funded by SSG, on the other hand, ensures that train providers have appropriate track record and processes to conduct training, that the trainers have requisite adult pedagogical training, and course contents fully cover the skills and competencies under the skills framework.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: There are four pillars in the Eco Stewardship Programme, namely Curriculum, Culture, Community and Campus.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: MOE will support schools in areas, such as emphasising sustainability in food production in our curriculum, and setting up of facilities for students to apply what they learnt on food production and food waste management.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: The IHLs will also continue to enhance skills training and research in sustainability related areas.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Mr Chairman, MOE is committed to building a culture of lifelong learning and equipping Singaporeans with the knowledge and skills that they need to thrive in school and at work.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: To this end, we will build on partnerships with the industry, unions, training providers, sector agencies and the community.
